title: Stagnation or Singularity?: Thiel's CS183 closing lecture on taking charge of the future
summary: Final CS183 class with futurist guests debating who builds the future and whether progress is inevitable. Thiel's own contributions: timing matters, and his closing call to treat your life as a singular event, find the many remaining secrets, and refuse the conventional path.

principles.text: The default path of safety and convention is the obvious answer, and it is wrong.
principles.quote: The obvious answer, unfortunately, has been to follow the well-trodden path. You are constantly encouraged to play it safe and be conventional.

principles.text: Many secrets remain; there are large unexplored areas of knowledge you can go discover.
principles.quote: By their nature, singular events are hard to teach or generalize about. But the big secret is that there are many secrets left to uncover.

principles.text: Treat your life and ventures as one-time events, not statistics.
principles.quote: Statistical processes, the law of large numbers, and globalization—these things are timeless, probabilistic, and maybe random. But, like technology, your life is a story of one-time events.

principles.text: 0 to 1 applies to your own life: every company or key decision is a singular event.
principles.quote: There is a mini singularity whenever you start a company or make a key life decision. In a very real sense, the life of every person is a singularity.

principles.text: Timing matters: working on a technology far too early is wasted effort.
principles.quote: No one was or should have been working on supersonic flight in the Middle Ages. That would be paddling way to far in advance of the wave.

principles.text: The future will not arrive on its own; you must take charge now.
principles.quote: If we don't take charge and usher in the future—if you don't take charge of your life—there is the sense that no one else will.
